originalTitle: Dropbox is a PC builder’s best friend
summary: In 2018 I bet my reputation and self-worth on a huge crowdfunded game design project. It could have been a failure for many reasons, but the one I became most worried about was losing all of the work that was stored locally on my home-built PC - a scenario that would have left a lot […]
content: In 2018 I bet my reputation and self-worth on a huge crowdfunded game design project. It could have been a failure for many reasons, but the one I became most worried about was losing all of the work that was stored locally on my home-built PC — a scenario that would have left a lot of people very upset and placed me in deep trouble. I wasn’t irresponsible, I had local backups, but at some point I found myself in custody of so many important files that it scared me. And no matter how many redundancies I could build at home, they’d all still be in the same place — a risky bet. So I bought a subscription to Dropbox. Years later, it’s still one of the best software subscriptions that I happily renew each year. It was great to have all that work backed up in the cloud — both for peace of mind and because it made working with collaborators breezier, letting them upload stuff directly to my drive, and letting me transfer files up to 50GB in size. In quick order I had built a trove of incredible artwork and complicated InDesign, Photoshop, and Illustrator files. The original goal for my Dropbox configuration was to make sure I wouldn’t lose any data in a worst-case scenario, so I set it up to mirror everything living on my work partition. Eventually, I ran smack into a worst-case scenario. Not once, but twice. I’m still not sure why, but my latest home-built PC chewed through two separate 2TB Samsung 970 Evo SSDs. It’s difficult to tell what went wrong with them, but in each case I woke up one morning to find when I tried to boot up that no drive could be detected. I can still feel my stomach trying to sink into the floor when I press that power button these days, never knowing if my drive had died in its sleep. Fortunately, both times, after some process-of-elimination testing I learned that just the drive had gone bad and everything else in my system was A-OK. Maybe I should have ditched Samsung after the second disaster, but I’m now on an 2TB 990 Evo Plus. Knock on wood, this thing better not fail. That drive now costs almost twice what I originally paid for it thanks to our new outrageously priced world of parts. My Dropbox bill is about $204 a year for a family plan ($17 a month), which includes up to six members. If you’re just in it for yourself you can get it for $9.99 a month billed yearly (about $120 a year), which comes with 2TB of storage. You can upgrade to 3TB for around $143 a year. That might be a tough sell for people who already have dozens of subscriptions, but I find it to be a decent price for excellent digital insurance. There are other powerful options out there, especially for professionals working with heavy files or complicated workflows. Backblaze, for example, has a personal backup plan with unlimited data for $99 a year and no restrictions on file size. And, of course, if you live on the Mac, Apple iCloud Plus isn’t a bad option — especially if you’re already paying for an Apple One subscription. Even Adobe offers file backups through Creative Cloud if that’s your jam, but I would not recommend using that clunky software suite for anything other than doing the work you need to do. I prefer Dropbox because the software works consistently well across multiple operating systems and is usually neither seen nor heard. The Windows client is snappy and I’ve found with a fast internet connection that its real-time syncing is efficient and painless. Anytime a file is modified in the partition I have mirrored in the cloud, Dropbox quietly begins uploading it and making changes to my mirrored files in the cloud. After using it for about eight years now I can’t recall a single time the service failed or faltered. It’s so fast and reliable I often forget it’s even there. Now, for the important caveat: This might not work for you if you have poor internet speeds. It really depends on how much data you’re regularly moving around on your computer and how quickly you make changes to it. This could particularly be a problem for asymmetrical data plans that commonly boast lightning-fast download speeds while offering pathetic upload speeds. I’ve done fine averaging only about 20Mbps upload, but if you’re on something even lower you should try a free trial for a backup plan before committing. You can also find plenty of download time calculators online; at my gigabit download speed it usually takes around two hours to download the 1TB of files I have synced in the cloud. And one more caveat: Putting everything (or even just many things) on your computer in the cloud isn’t for everyone, and I completely understand why many folks wouldn’t or shouldn’t do that for sensitive files. I once built local RAID drives and even airgapped storage systems to avoid having everything online. These things are still possible but getting more expensive by the day as storage prices spike. You’re the best judge of how and where your data should be protected. That sinking feeling of potentially losing my whole PC? It was immediately followed each time by the assurance that I’d only lost a computer’s body and not its soul. When I got my PC back up and running with new storage, it ended up taking less time to resync all my files than it did to troubleshoot and install new hardware. I can almost hear Billy Crudup doing a Mastercard commercial in my head: New solid state drive, three hundred eighty-nine dollars. Yearly Dropbox subscription, two hundred and three dollars. Never worrying about losing your data? Priceless.
chineseTitle: Dropbox 是 PC 制造商最好的朋友
chineseSummary: 2018年，我把自己的声誉和自我价值押在了一个巨大的众筹游戏设计项目上。由于多种原因，它可能会失败，但我最担心的是丢失本地存储在我自制 PC 上的所有工作 - 这种情况会留下很多 [...]
chineseContent: 2018年，我把自己的声誉和自我价值押在了一个巨大的众筹游戏设计项目上。由于多种原因，它可能会失败，但我最担心的是丢失本地存储在我自制 PC 上的所有工作 - 这种情况会让很多人非常沮丧，并使我陷入深深的麻烦。我并不是不负责任，我有本地备份，但在某些时候我发现自己保管着如此多的重要文件，这让我感到害怕。无论我在家里裁员多少，他们仍然会在同一个地方——这是一个冒险的赌注。所以我订阅了 Dropbox。多年后，它仍然是我每年都很高兴续订的最好的软件订阅之一。将所有工作都备份在云中真是太棒了——既可以让您安心，又可以让与协作者的合作变得更加轻松，让他们可以将内容直接上传到我的驱动器，并让我可以传输最大 50GB 的文件。我很快就构建了一系列令人难以置信的艺术作品和复杂的 InDesign、Photoshop 和 Illustrator 文件。我的 Dropbox 配置的最初目标是确保在最坏的情况下不会丢失任何数据，因此我将其设置为镜像工作分区上的所有内容。最终，我遇到了最坏的情况。不是一次，而是两次。我仍然不知道为什么，但我最新的自制 PC 消耗了两个独立的 2TB 三星 970 Evo SSD。很难说出它们出了什么问题，但在每种情况下，我有一天早上醒来时都发现，当我尝试启动时，无法检测到任何驱动器。这些天，当我按下电源按钮时，我仍然能感觉到我的胃试图沉入地板，永远不知道我的驱动器是否在睡眠中死掉了。幸运的是，两次都经过一些消除过程测试
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于 AI 与科技趋势信号，适合用于观察工具选型、产品机会、开发者关注点和技术路线变化。
